activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
story:
Blake's problem was simple and maddening: Mrs. Toro's computer science class was building a prime checker by Friday, and his program kept calling 9 a prime. He had dragged his laptop to Devon's basement, where the couch smelled like popcorn and the ping-pong table held more laundry than paddles.

"Run it again," Devon said, wedging himself between a laundry basket and a stack of board games. Blake typed 9 and hit Enter. PRIME, the screen announced, confident and wrong.

"It's the loop," Blake muttered. He scrolled up, scanning the code he'd written at midnight. His program asked for a number, then checked whether anything divided it evenly, but somewhere in the loop it skipped the checking entirely, like a security guard waving everyone through. "It says nine is prime, which means it's broken, which means I don't actually know if any of my answers are right."

Devon tossed him a marker. "Then don't trust the machine. Trust paper." He pulled a whiteboard from behind the furnace and drew a grid, numbers 2 through 30 across it in careful rows. "My grandpa showed me this once. It's called the Sieve of Eratosthenes."

"The what?"

"An ancient Greek method. You list the numbers, then cross out the multiples of each prime in turn. Watch." Devon circled the 2, then crossed out 4, 6, 8, all the way down the board. Then he circled 3 and crossed out its multiples, 9 among them, already X-ed from the 2 pass but getting a second, grimmer X. "Five, seven, and so on. Whatever survives, survives because it's prime."

Blake copied the grid into his notebook, stubborn number by stubborn number, and held it up beside his screen. Every answer the program printed for the numbers he tested, 29, 23, 17, matched the survivors on the grid. Then he typed 9. PRIME. He typed 25. PRIME. The program was an obstinate little liar, but at least now he had proof, and proof meant he could hunt the bug instead of guessing.

He read the loop aloud, line by line, and stopped. "The range starts at the number itself instead of below it, so nothing ever divides it, so everything looks prime." He deleted one character, changed the range, and typed 9. NOT PRIME. He typed 25. NOT PRIME. He typed 29. PRIME. He checked each one against the whiteboard grid, where 29 sat uncircled and uncrossed, a survivor.

"Devon. I'm going to replicate this exact grid for every number from 2 to 100 and test all of it." Blake was already drawing a second notebook page. Devon groaned, but he picked up the marker anyway and started a fresh column at 31.

"That makes you the world's slowest computer," Devon said.

"Slow," Blake agreed, crossing out his first multiple, "but never wrong."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
Jackson stared at his blank page and wished his characters would just shut up, except they weren't talking at all. His rough draft was all summary: Maya went to the lake, then Maya found the boat, then Maya got scared. Mr. Ruiz had circled three paragraphs and written "Where is the dialogue? Where is your climax?" in aggressive red ink that made the paper look like it had been in a fight.

Across the table, Priya flipped her worksheet over and sketched a jagged line climbing upward. "Mine looks like a mountain," she said. "The climax is the peak." She tapped the top of her drawing. "It's called Freytag's pyramid. My cousin told me about it. It comes from a guy named Gustav Freytag who wrote a book on drama in 1863." She drew the line falling down the other side. "The plot rises to the climax at the peak, then falls after."

Jackson borrowed her pencil and drew his own mountain under Priya's, because hers left room. "So my story's been flat." He plotted dots along the slope. "Maya hears a noise at the bottom. Then she sees the boat. Then the boat drifts loose with her little brother on it, and that's the peak." He tested the idea by rereading his draft. Every event sat on the low ground, bunched together. That was why the story felt like a list instead of a climb.

He started rewriting at the lake itself. "What are you doing out here?" Maya called. Her brother's voice came back thin over the water: "Getting the rope off the propeller." Jackson remembered the rules from the board, quotation marks around the words, comma before the tag, new paragraph whenever the speaker changed. He messed it up twice and fixed it, and Priya leaned over.

"Your dialogue does the rising now," she said. "Every line makes it worse for Maya. That's the climb." She pointed at his peak. "You could nominate the brother to shout something scary right there. Like the motor starting by itself." Jackson laughed and wrote it: "It's going, Maya, it's going, I can't reach the key!" The fall came fast after that, Maya swimming, the rope, the shallow water, the two of them coughing on the bank.

Mr. Ruiz walked the rows and stopped at their table. He read Jackson's page, then the mountain on the back of Priya's worksheet, and his eyebrows went up. "You made an inference from a drawing," he said. "Not bad." He set a sticky note beside Jackson's climax: Read aloud to the class? Jackson looked at Priya, who gave him a thumbs up, and he wrote one word under the note: Yes.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
story:
Every night before the canoe trip, Alyssa's stomach felt tight and upset, and on Tuesday she could not fall asleep until the raccoons outside the cabin were already raiding the marshmallow bag. She assumed the bug was going around camp. But when she thought about it, the stomachaches had started the exact day Ms. Ruiz posted the sign-up sheet for the canoe trip, and they seemed to orbit that sheet the way the moths orbited the porch light. That was a pattern. Patterns meant something.

On Wednesday night the stomachache came back, along with sweaty palms, and by Thursday she had a headache too, right behind her eyes. Three symptoms. Her bunkmate Dree leaned down from the top bunk and said, "You look like a ghost that lost its sheet."

"I feel like a ghost that lost its whole laundry," Alyssa said. She held up her hands. "Look. Sweaty palms. Again."

Dree climbed down and sat on the edge of the lower bunk. "My cousin used to get stomachaches every Sunday night," she said. "And a pharmacist asked her mom if something big happened at school on Mondays. It turned out it was stress. Stress can show up in the body like that. Headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms, trouble falling asleep. She had basically the whole menu."

Alyssa lay back and stared at the ceiling. She was not sick. She was stressed, and her body was reporting it like a walkie-talkie. But that raised a question she could actually test. If stress was causing the trouble falling asleep, maybe she could do something about it. The next afternoon she found Ms. Ruiz, who had told everyone on day one that she was there as their mentor, not their boss. "Can I ask you something that isn't about canoes?" Alyssa said. "How do you calm down before something scary?"

Ms. Ruiz laughed. "Slow breathing. In for four, out for six. I do it before I drive over that narrow bridge to town, and I used to be aggressive about honking at anyone who slowed me down on it."

That night, Alyssa tried the breathing in her bunk. In for four, out for six, while her brain insisted the canoe would tip and the lake was full of imaginary sharks. She also made a routine: same order every night, teeth, bag packed for morning, flashlight off at exactly nine. On Friday she fell asleep before the raccoons even clocked in. On Saturday her stomach was quiet and her hands were dry, and she paddled the whole lake without tipping, although Dree splashed her once with an aggressive backstroke on purpose.

"See?" Dree shouted from the other canoe. "No stomachache!"

"No menu!" Alyssa shouted back, and dipped her paddle into the cold green water.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
story:
Claire spread the photocopy on the study table and read the first line for the fifth time. "To be, or not to be, that is the question." The library smelled like warm paper and floor wax, and somewhere behind her a copier hummed and clunked, patient as a heartbeat. She had until five o'clock, when the doors locked, and her English test was first period Monday. The assignment said to paraphrase the speech into her own words, and so far all she had written was "Should I be, or should I not be," which she knew was wrong.

The strange part was that Hamlet wasn't talking to anyone. In the scenes before, characters traded lines back and forth like players passing a ball, but here the stage directions just said he enters alone. Claire flipped pages, hunting for the person he must be addressing. Nobody. She leaned closer, as if the missing listener were hiding between the lines of print.

A boy from her class, Marcus, dropped into the chair across from her with his own photocopy and a granola bar. "You stuck too?" he asked, unwrapping it in loud crinkles. She slid her paper toward him. "He's just talking," she said. "To nobody. For thirty-one lines. People don't do that." Marcus chewed and squinted at the page. "There's a word for it," he said. "My sister had it last year. A soliloquy is a speech where a character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts aloud so the audience can hear them."

Claire sat back. She tried an experiment, the kind her science teacher called testing a hypothesis. If the speech was private thoughts spoken aloud, then Hamlet wasn't telling another character anything. He was telling her. She read the line again, slower, hearing it as a secret passed across the footlights: should he keep living, or end it. The cold feeling in her stomach said she'd finally cracked the door open. She picked up her pencil and wrote, "Should I keep living or give up," then kept going, line by line, turning each old phrase into plain speech while the idea stayed consistent with what he actually said.

At four forty the lights over the stacks blinked once, the librarian's warning that the building was closing. Claire's hand ached and her paraphrase was almost done, but the last lines were the hardest, tangled and strange. She read them under her breath, listened to the sound of them, and tried again. "Love survives a little while, then fades," she wrote, deciding that captured it.

Marcus peered over, granola crumbs on his sleeve. "You think that's what he means?" Claire checked the original one more time, holding her version beside it, comparing. Then she underlined her answer, folded the paper, and dropped it into her backpack as the lights blinked a second time. "Read it yourself," she said. "We've got fifteen minutes."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
story:
The rain began just after they finished pitching the tent, and Penelope spread her two printed satellite images across the picnic table under the tarp, weighting the corners with pinecones. The picture on the left showed Asia in January. The one on the right showed the same continent in July. Her best friend Rumela crouched beside her, arms crossed against the drizzle, waiting.

"Your mom really farms rice back there?" Rumela asked, and Penelope nodded. Last summer, during the video call, her grandmother had stood in a flooded paddy field and held the phone low so Penelope could see the water catching the sky. That field needed the rain, her grandmother had said, or the rice would not grow, and Penelope had promised to understand it properly before the family visited next year.

"I keep getting it wrong in practice," Penelope said. "My presentation just says rains come, then rice grows. That's not an explanation. That's a weather report with a plant stuck on the end." She tapped the January image. "Look here. There's a band of clouds around the middle of the Earth, near the equator. It's like a belt." She ran her finger along the bright white streak crossing the ocean below India. Then she moved her hand to the July image and stopped. The belt had moved. It sat farther north, draped over South Asia itself, right where her grandmother's fields were.

Rumela leaned in, rain dripping off the tarp between them. "So in January the band is down here," she said, pointing at the equator, "and in July it's up over India. What's it called?"

"The Intertropical Convergence Zone," Penelope said. "It's a rainy band of rising air." She stood very still, because the pieces were lining up in her head the way knots line up before they come undone. The band shifted north in the northern summer. The band was rainy. When it shifted over South Asia, the rains came with it. That was the monsoon, arriving because the band had moved, not out of nowhere. "That's why the rains come when they come," she said slowly. "The whole thing follows the band."

She grabbed a pencil and, on the back of a permission slip, drew a rough map with a cloud stripe, then sketched the same map again with the stripe pushed upward, the two drawings side by side and almost symmetrical. "I can show these on the projector and let everyone watch it move," she said. "Nobody has to take my word for it. They can see it themselves." She thought of her grandmother standing in the flooded field, the crop rising out of water that had traveled halfway up a continent. "If I mess this up in class, I can't exactly retire from being half-Indian," she said, and Rumela laughed. "The protagonist of this presentation is the cloud band anyway. I'm just the narrator."

The rain drummed harder on the tarp. Penelope slid both images into a plastic sleeve, zipped it into her pack, and said, "Rice and rain. One follows the other. Grandmother, you're getting a good report this time."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Elliot stood in the synagogue library with his reading packet in one hand and a pencil in the other, staring at the same Hebrew line for the fourth time. In two weeks he would chant his bar mitzvah portion in front of everyone, and so far he had memorized exactly one and a half verses out of nine.

"You look like a boy who lost his shoes," said Mr. Adler, who shelved books on Tuesdays. He was not the rabbi, just a man who liked quiet and order.

"I keep saying it and it disappears," Elliot said. "I'll get a line perfect, then the next one contradicts it in my head. Same words, different order, and my brain picks the wrong one every time."

Mr. Adler tapped the packet. "My grandmother used the method of loci," he said. "Ask your mother what it means. Or figure it out yourself, which is better." Then he wheeled his cart away, which was how he ended most conversations.

That night, Elliot sprawled on his grandmother's living room rug while she knitted in her chair. He told her the problem: nine verses, all tangled, a contradiction between every other pair of lines in his memory. She set down her needles.

"Try my house," she said. "Walk through it in your mind. You know every corner."

So he did. First verse went at the front door, where the mezuzah sat at a tilt nobody fixed. Second verse in the hallway with the mirror. Third on the kitchen table, next to the bowl of walnuts. Fourth in the pantry, fifth on the basement stairs, sixth by the washing machine, seventh in the sewing room, eighth under her humming ceiling fan, ninth at the back door with its sticky handle. He placed each line in its spot and said it there, out loud, until the words seemed to belong to the walnuts and the mirror and the stairs.

The next morning he tested it. He closed his eyes and walked the route in his mind: door, mezuzah, hallway, mirror, kitchen, walnuts. Each verse rose up out of its place, in order, whole. He walked the route three times without a single slip, and when his grandmother shuffled in with tea, he recited all nine verses standing in her actual kitchen, grinning like the fan above him had made him buoyant.

On the bimah two weeks later, Elliot closed his eyes for half a second, saw a tilted mezuzah, and began. His voice held steady through the pantry and the sewing room and the sticky back door, and when he finished, Mr. Adler nodded once from the third row. After the service, Elliot's little sister tugged his sleeve.

"How did you remember all that?"

"Meet me at Grandma's," he said. "I'll give you the tour."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like coffee and toast, and the kettle was sending thin curls of vapor toward the ceiling when Madison opened her laptop. Grandma slid a plate of biscuits beside her and said, "The principal wants my survey numbers by seven tonight, sweetpea. Two hundred kids answered, and I can't make heads or tails of the list." Madison had promised she could do it. She had watched one video about pivot tables last night, twice, and she figured that was enough.

She dragged the Grade column into the rows area, then dragged Answers into values, and the spreadsheet snapped everything into tidy counts: sixth grade, seventh grade, eighth grade. And then a fourth row she had not asked for. "Grandma, is there a fourth grade at your school?" Grandma leaned over her shoulder, squinting. "There is not." The extra row sat there in gray letters, labeled "(blank)", with eleven kids in it.

Madison tapped the table with her pen. A hidden cause, she thought, like a draft you can't see moving the curtains. She could infer what it meant, or she could test it. She went back to the raw list and sorted the Grade column, scrolling until the empty cells clustered together at the bottom. Eleven of them. Eleven rows where somebody had answered the survey question but left the grade box untouched. Eleven kids who skipped it. The counts matched exactly. She sat back so fast the chair squeaked.

"Those eleven didn't write their grade down," she said. "So the table gives them their own group, "(blank)"". Grandma laughed and patted the table like it had done her a favor. "Skippers. Every school has them." She copied the numbers onto a lined pad for her meeting, and her handwriting was quick and sure, the way it used to be before the tremor came.

The clock over the stove said six forty when Madison added the totals to Grandma's notes, checked them twice, and emailed everything to the principal. Grandma hugged her, then stood a moment at the window with the pad still in her hand, and Madison saw her mouth the numbers silently, rehearsing, the way she did now to keep hold of things. There had been a time Grandma would have presented without notes at all, without needing anybody.

"You'll come with me Thursday?" Grandma asked. "You can fix it if the laptop fusses." Madison said yes, even though Thursday was the night of the recital she'd been practicing for since September. The kitchen light hummed. Grandma poured the last of the coffee, and the steam rose off the cup and vanished before it reached the ceiling.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
story:
Asher sat cross-legged on the rug in Theo's basement, balancing a laptop on his knees while the furnace rattled behind the wall. Copper pipes ran across the ceiling, and someone had wrapped the ones near the water heater in foam to insulate them, though Asher could not have said why he noticed that now. His eyes were stuck on the screen, where the words "not prime" scrolled down the terminal in a long, relentless column.

"It did it again," he said. "Fifty times."

Theo leaned over from the beanbag chair, crunching a pretzel. "Type in forty-nine again."

Asher typed it. The program asked for a number, he entered 49, and the machine replied "not prime" for every divisor it tested: 7 printed "not prime," then 7 again, and on and on until the loop finished counting all the way up. One number in, fifty lines out. "It's not wrong," Asher said slowly. "Forty-nine isn't prime. But it keeps checking after it already knows."

He scrolled back through his own code, tracing the loop with one finger against the screen. The program tested each possible divisor from 2 upward, and each time one divided evenly it printed "not prime" and then, because nothing told it to stop, it went right on testing. The rule was hiding somewhere in that gap between knowing and stopping. He tried typing "quit" after the print statement, which only crashed the whole program with an error in red.

Theo tossed him a folded note from the desk, where they had been passing messages all afternoon because Theo's little sister kept eavesdropping at the top of the stairs. Asher unfolded it. "Ask my cousin," it read. "He taught himself all this. He's eccentric but he knows everything." Below that Theo had scribbled his cousin's handle. Asher sent one message: "my prime checker prints not prime 50 times for one number. how do i make it stop after the first divisor?"

The reply came fast. "You need a break statement. A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor."

Asher added one word after the print line, saved, and ran it again. He typed 49. The terminal printed "not prime" exactly once and sat quiet. Then he tried 97, and the word "prime" appeared, single and clean, like a coin landing heads. He tried 2, then 91, then a number he made up on the spot, watching each answer arrive without chatter.

"Theo," he said. "Come look at this."

Theo peered at the screen, pretzel halfway to his mouth. "Okay, that's satisfying. Try the biggest one you know."

Asher's fingers hovered over the keyboard, and somewhere above them the pipes ticked as heat moved through the conductor inside them. He started typing digits and had not decided yet when to stop.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
story:
Edouard balanced his notebook on his knees as the bus rattled toward the science center. Every Thursday, the six members of the Inventors Club met on the long ride to their workshop, and today was the first time he would run the meeting himself. He had typed an agenda the night before: tinker at the old item first, then vote on the new project, then assign jobs. His friend Sam leaned over the seat and read it upside down.

"An agenda," Sam said. "Very official."

"It's so everyone gets a chance to speak," Edouard said. "Even quiet people like Priya."

The meeting started well. Priya reported that the club had finally managed to acquire the small motor they needed, which meant the robot arm could actually be built. Then Marcus raised his hand, which was good, except that what he said had nothing to do with the robot arm. He wanted to build a cat feeder out of the old cereal dispenser. The whole bus seat erupted into an argument about whether cats would even use it.

"Back to item two," Edouard said. "The vote on the new project."

They got thirty seconds of voting before Yasmin remembered a component she had seen at the hobby shop, a wheel that glowed in the dark, and suddenly everyone was debating glow-in-the-dark wheels. Every time Edouard dragged them back, another idea burst loose like a leak in a boat. He noticed a pattern: it was never the quiet members who derailed things. Priya had spoken exactly once. The loud voices were the chronic ones, speaking over and over, and the good ideas that pulled them off track were almost always the loud ones too.

So Edouard tested a simple idea. Instead of shutting Marcus and Yasmin down, which just made them louder, he wrote their ideas down in a list at the back of his notebook. Marcus's cat feeder. Yasmin's glowing wheels.

"What's that part of the agenda?" Sam asked.

"It's called a parking lot," Edouard said. "A list where the meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later, instead of derailing the current item."

Marcus squinted at it, then sat back, satisfied that his idea was safely stored somewhere. Yasmin stopped talking, because she could see her wheels sitting on the page, waiting for her. The bus went quiet in a strange new way, and in that quiet, Priya raised her hand.

"I think the cat feeder could be the next project," she said. "But the robot arm is due Friday. If we finish the arm first, Marcus's feeder could use the leftover motor mounts."

Nobody interrupted her. Marcus actually wrote that down.

At the workshop, the vote took four minutes, and the club finished the robot arm with time left to sketch the feeder. On the ride home, Priya tapped Edouard's notebook.

"Your parking lot," she said. "Can I run the meeting next week?"

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
The sunflower seeds in Addison's cup were the only thing she had managed to grow all summer, and even those had just begun to germinate, tiny pale hooks pushing out of the soil on the camp's nature shelf. She checked them every morning before breakfast, mostly to avoid the table where Dex Turner sat. For the third day in a row, Dex had dumped Noah's tray supplies into the mud, called him "Shrimp Boy," and laughed while his two friends laughed with him. Noah was smaller than everyone, and he never said anything back. Addison kept deciding it wasn't her business, and every night the decision sat in her chest like a stone.

On Thursday she watched Marcus and Ben argue over a paddle by the canoe dock. They shouted, shoved each other once, and then Marcus said, "Fine, take it," and they were laughing again by lunch. That was when the pieces started fitting together in Addison's head. One argument, between two boys who were basically equal, ended on its own. What happened to Noah was different. It happened again and again, and it was always three against one.

"So it's not the same thing at all," she said to Noah at the craft table, keeping her voice low.

"Not the same as what?" Noah asked, weaving a lanyard with frail, careful fingers.

"Marcus and Ben fighting. That's just a one-time thing between equals. What those guys do to you is repeated, and they've got all the power because there's three of them and one of you." She picked up a strand of plastic lace. "My cousin told me researchers actually define it that way. If it's repeated and there's an imbalance of power, it's bullying."

Noah's hands stopped moving. "I thought it was just joking," he said quietly.

"That's what he wants you to think," Addison said. She felt the guilt of three silent mornings rise up, and she made herself a promise about it. "Here's my idea. We don't fight him. We just make sure you're never alone, and we tell Counselor Rivera exactly what happened, with dates. Repeated things leave a pattern, and patterns are easy to prove."

On Friday, Dex reached for Noah's water bottle at the archery range, and Addison stepped into his path. "You've done something to him every single day this week," she said, loud enough that the group turned. "Counselor Rivera has the whole list." Dex's two friends looked at their shoes. Dex shoved his hands in his pockets and walked off toward the target shed, alone.

Noah shot an arrow that landed near the center of the target. Then he turned to Addison and asked, "Did the sunflower seeds sprout this morning?"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
story:
Grayson slid his copy of the story across the library table so the others could see the paragraph he had flagged with a sticky note. The book club met in the corner by the window, seven folding chairs and a box of pretzels nobody touched until the arguing started. Today they were arguing, and it was mostly his fault.

"You said the ending came out of nowhere," Priya said, flipping back to page one. "But you wrote 'why' next to the first paragraph, like, five times."

"That was before I finished it," Grayson said. His pencil taps slowed. "Read the first paragraph again. Out loud."

Priya read it. It was all sunshine and flowers, school just out for the summer, and then, without any fuss, the children collecting stones, gathering them into piles, guarding them. Grayson watched his friends' faces change as the words landed on them a second time. Marcus actually leaned back like the page had pushed him.

"They're stacking rocks," Marcus said. "That's just kids being kids."

"Is it, though?" Grayson said. "Jackson published this in The New Yorker in 1948. She could have opened with the weather, the food, anything. She picked stones." He hadn't planned to say that out loud; he'd found it himself at midnight, rereading the calm opening after the ending had knocked him flat. The whole lottery had been sitting there in paragraph one, patient as a trap.

Priya turned the page face down, then face up again, as if the stones might have changed. "So the rocks at the start are... foreshadowing."

"That's the word," Grayson said. He wrote it in the margin. His older sister had used it about a movie once and he'd pretended to know what she meant. He thought about all the times he'd done that, nodded along, kept his questions in his pocket where they couldn't embarrass him. He was trying to stop doing that, one small test at a time. "And maybe the black box is a symbol. A vessel, kind of. It carries the whole tradition inside it, and nobody remembers why anymore."

"The village doesn't even have anything to win," Priya said quietly. "That's the barren part. No prize, just the ritual."

Marcus picked up a pretzel, held it like a stone, and dropped it into the empty pretzel bag. It landed with a soft click.

"Okay," he said. "So if the stones show up in the first paragraph, what else did she bury in there?"

Grayson looked down at page one again and put his pencil where the first sentence began.

story:
"Dude, I'm going to find the biggest prime number ever," Henry announced, dropping his backpack next to Marcus's basement couch. "And then they'll name it after me."

Marcus spun around in his desk chair, laptop open, a bag of chips between his knees. "You can't. Also, we're supposed to be writing your Python program today, remember? The prime checker? For extra credit?"

"That's exactly the plan." Henry pulled out his notebook, already covered in numbers. "The program tests if a number is prime. So I test bigger and bigger numbers until I find one so big nobody's ever tested it. Boom. Henry's Prime." He cracked his knuckles like he was about to lift something heavy.

Marcus chewed a chip and watched his friend open the laptop. The basement smelled like popcorn and old carpet, and the ceiling fan clicked in its slow, chronic way, a sound Marcus's dad kept promising to fix and never did. Henry typed fast, tongue between his teeth.

"I'm asking for a number," he explained, "and then the program checks if anything divides into it. If nothing does, it's prime."

"Okay, but you have to tell it how to check," Marcus said, leaning over. "It's not just going to know."

That was the part that provoked Henry into actually thinking instead of just typing. A number either had divisors or it didn't, but the computer couldn't see that. It had to try dividing, one number at a time, like feeling around a dark room. He wrote a loop, dividing by two, then three, then four, and if any division came out even, the number failed. If the loop survived all the way through, it was prime.

"Try nine," Marcus said.

Henry typed nine and hit enter. NOT PRIME, the screen said.

"Try eleven."

PRIME.

Henry whooped so loud Marcus's dog barked upstairs. They tested a hundred, then a thousand and nine, then six thousand fifty-three, which turned out to be prime, and Henry wrote it on his arm with a pen because his notebook was across the room and that seemed too far to walk.

Then he typed a number with twelve digits. The cursor blinked. The fan clicked. The screen just sat there, thinking, and Henry's heart started thumping like the program was a racehorse he'd bet on. Finally: PRIME.

"Okay, that's a big one," Marcus said. "Is it the biggest?"

Henry started typing a bigger one, then a way bigger one, digits spilling across the line like a runaway train. Somewhere in the middle of all this, Marcus's older sister came down to do laundry, saw the screen, and laughed.

"You know there's no biggest prime, right?"

"There has to be," Henry said. "There's a biggest everything."

"Not primes." She shoved clothes into the washer. "Euclid proved it. Around 300 BC. He wrote it in this book, the Elements. Infinitely many primes. They just never stop."

Henry stared at her, then at his screen, where his giant number sat with PRIME glowing under it. He felt a strange dip, like missing the last step on a staircase. No Henry's Prime. No naming ceremony. His whole plan had a hole in it the size of forever.

He sat back down anyway. His twelve-digit prime was still up there, still real, still his, even if it wasn't the last one. "Fine," he said. "Then I'll find a bigger one than anyone at school has ever seen."

"That's the spirit," Marcus said, and Henry's fingers were already back on the keys.

"Give me a number with twenty digits."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Camille sat cross-legged on the carpeted floor of the gurdwara with the Gutka open on her knees, the Gurmukhi letters swimming a little whenever she got tired. In two weeks she would kneel at the Khalsa initiation ceremony, and part of preparing for it was knowing Japji Sahib, the morning prayer, by heart. She had most of it. But there was one passage, a long roll of lines near the middle, where her tongue always tripped, and today it tripped four times in a row.

"You're rushing it," said her cousin Simran, who was twelve and had memorized the whole thing in a month. "Slow down."

"I'm not rushing. It just collapses." Camille closed the book. In third grade she had once given up on a school poem and stood silent in front of the whole class, and she remembered standing there, cheeks burning, deciding she would never memorize anything again. She had kept that promise for years. Now she was breaking it, and she hadn't told anyone that the old fear was part of why she kept stumbling.

She tried an experiment. Instead of repeating the passage out loud, she whispered it while walking the long hallway outside the langar hall, matching one line to each two steps. When a line still slid away from her, she modified the plan: three steps for the hard lines, two for the easy ones. Something about the rhythm held the words in place, the way a paper propeller she had once folded caught the air and rose instead of fluttering down.

Near the shoe shelves she found her mother's sister, Auntie Ji, tying a scarf over her hair. "Simran says the new initiates recite Japji Sahib at the ceremony," Camille said. "Why that one?"

"It's called Amrit Sanchar," Auntie Ji said, straightening the scarf. "And yes, Japji Sahib is recited there." She smiled a little. "It's the first thing Guru Nanak sang, and it's the first prayer of the morning. Ask your mother what it was like."

Camille had assumed her mother had sailed through her own initiation without a single mistake, because that was how her mother seemed to do everything. But that evening, at the kitchen table, her mother laughed. "The middle passage," she said. "I forgot it completely at my Amrit Sanchar. I stood there in front of everyone, and then I whispered the lines, and nobody minded. The point isn't being perfect, Camille. The point is showing up with it in your heart."

Camille looked down at her Gutka. Her mother, silent in front of everyone. It made the old classroom memory feel smaller, somehow, and the coming ceremony feel less like a test. She turned back to the middle passage and read it aloud, slowly, her foot tapping twice for every line beneath the table. When she reached the end without stopping, she looked up and said, "Again. Time me this time."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
Lillian set her backpack on the kitchen table next to a plate of celery sticks, which her little brother Gus immediately claimed as his own even though they were plainly hers. "I need you to be Marcus Welch," she said.

"Who?" Gus crunched a stalk.

"A kid at school. He wears the same dinosaur shirt every Tuesday, and today Derek told him he looked like a herbivore who lost a fight. Everyone laughed, including me." The celery tasted suddenly bitter in her mouth. "I laughed because it was easier than saying something, and Marcus saw me do it."

Gus, who was ten and took assignments seriously, pulled his hood up and said in a deep voice, "Nice shirt, herbivore." He even pointed, his finger crooked in a way that was symmetrical, like a mirror image of Derek's actual crooked finger. That small accuracy made her wince.

"Okay, so what do I say back?" Lillian had been turning this over all afternoon. In health class they'd read about a 2001 study of school playgrounds, and one line had stuck to her like a burr: when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases. Not always. Not even most of the time, if you were strict about the words. More than half. She'd expected to feel discouraged by that, but instead she kept thinking that more than half was a lot of Tuesdays.

Here was her idea, and she wanted to test it before she used it on a real person: the reason Derek teased Marcus wasn't Marcus at all, which meant defending Marcus might provoke Derek into doubling down. So maybe the move wasn't to confront Derek. Maybe it was to walk toward Marcus instead, to stand next to him, to talk to him like the joke hadn't landed at all. If the audience disappeared, maybe the teasing would too.

She tried it. "Hey, Marcus," she said to the empty air beside the refrigerator, "did you finish the science homework? I got stuck on number four and you're the only one who actually reads the whole worksheet." Gus, still in character as Derek, opened his mouth to say something mean, then found there was nobody to say it to. His finger drooped. He looked from Lillian to the refrigerator and back, visibly unsure what he was supposed to do now.

"That felt weird," Lillian said, "but not bad-weird."

Gus pulled his hood down. "You ignored me. That was the whole trick?"

"That was the whole trick. Tomorrow I'm going to stand next to Marcus and ask him about the homework, and if Derek tries again, he's talking to a wall." She took back her celery. At lunch she slid her tray next to Marcus's, and when Derek looked over, she was already asking, "Number four, did you get it?"

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
story:
Lydia stood in front of the phone case kiosk at Westfield Mall holding the display model of the phone she wanted, the one with the camera good enough to actually matter, and did the math she'd been avoiding. Six hundred dollars. Her savings account held one hundred forty.

Her mother worked at the bank branch by the food court, and the manager had a rule about employees' kids hanging around: they could sit in the back office as long as they didn't obstruct the hallway or touch the copier. Lydia sat in the back office now, because the kiosk made the six hundred dollars feel urgent and the office had a calculator with a power key.

"Are you still doing the thing with your birthday money?" her mother asked, poking her head in.

"Trying to see what it turns into by graduation," Lydia said. She had the bank's rate sheet, which said 5 percent yearly, compounded once a year. Simple interest, she'd figured out on her own, meant the same five dollars every year on her hundred, so after five years she'd have one hundred twenty-five. That part felt honest, almost boring.

Then she typed 1.05 and hit the power key with 5. The screen said 1.2762815625. She frowned at it, wrote it down, and multiplied by her hundred. One hundred twenty-seven and change. Two dollars and sixty-three cents more than simple interest, just sitting there.

"That's compound," said Denzel, a tenant from the smoothie stand who came through the office every afternoon to cash his checks. He leaned on the doorframe. "You're earning interest on your interest."

"Is that legal?" Lydia asked.

"It's the whole business model," Denzel said, and went back to his blender.

Lydia tried it with different numbers. Four years, three years, six. The power key didn't care; it just did the same multiplication over and over and handed her the answer. She tried 8 percent, and the gap between simple and compound got wider. She tried starting with five hundred instead of one hundred, and the gap got wider again. Somewhere in there, she stopped thinking about the phone and started thinking about the pattern.

At closing time her mother found her still in the chair, calculator warm in her hands, an entire napkin covered with powers.

"Did you figure out the phone?" her mother asked.

"Better," Lydia said. "I figured out that if I put in fifty dollars a month for five years, compound interest does half my saving for me." She held up the napkin. "I'm going to be so optimistic about this that I might even skip the mall next Saturday."

Her mother looked at the napkin, then at her. "You said that about the smoothie diet too."

"I know," Lydia said, and typed 1.05 one more time, just to watch it.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
story:
Juliette slid her notebook across the cafe table so Marta could see it, then wished she hadn't, because Marta's eyebrows went up in a way that promised ridicule before she'd read a single line. The writing club had claimed the corner booth again, four mugs and one shared lemon pound cake between them, and tomorrow every member had to turn in a one-page essay with a real argument in it.

"My thesis is that homework makes students tired," Marta announced, tapping her pen. "Done. Now I just need three points."

"Everyone knows homework makes you tired," said Dev, without looking up from his laptop.

"Exactly. It's true." Marta spread her hands, triumphant.

Juliette looked down at her own page, where she'd written and crossed out the same sentence three times: School starts too early for teenagers. Her hand ached and her eyes had that gritty fatigue that came from staring at one line for forty minutes. Something about Marta's thesis was bothering her, and she couldn't name it yet.

"Play it out," she said slowly, testing the idea the way she'd test a wobbly table, by pressing on it. "Imagine a hypothetical reader. You say homework makes students tired. Who says no? Who argues back?"

"Nobody," Marta said. "Because it's obvious."

"So what's your essay for? You're just telling people something they already agree with." Juliette felt the thought click into place. "A thesis has to be a claim a reasonable person could disagree with. If it's just a plain fact nobody would dispute, there's nothing to argue. Nothing for your three points to do."

Dev finally looked up. "Then what's a good one?"

Marta chewed her cake and stared at the window. "Homework should be banned entirely," she tried.

Juliette laughed. "Okay, that one, plenty of people would fight you on that."

Marta rewrote her thesis at the top of a fresh page, and Dev started typing fast, and the club felt like a club again, everyone building at once. Juliette turned back to her own paper. School starts too early, she wrote, then crossed it out and kept going: School should start later even if it means sports practice ends in the dark. Her grandmother would say it was a waste of a Saturday afternoon, arguing on paper about school hours when she could be outside.

That night her mother read the thesis over her shoulder and frowned. "Later starts? Then I'd have to drive you in the dark instead of the light. I'd argue with that."

Juliette grinned and underlined the sentence twice.

"Good," her mother said, handing the page back. "You realize your father disagrees completely, though. He loves early starts."

Juliette sat very still. The one reasonable person guaranteed to be at her breakfast table every morning for the next four years was now her essay's perfect audience, and he was also the last person on earth she wanted to win against.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Samantha spread two climate graphs across the counter of Sunrise Travel, where her Aunt Rosa worked on Saturdays. One graph showed the Sahara, with rainfall bars so short they looked like a row of commas and temperatures that climbed every summer. The other showed the Amazon, with tall rainfall bars stacked month after month. Her assignment was due Monday, and her plan was simple: use the agency's big globe to match each graph to a place, then write it up.

The trouble was her dad, who was taking her to Peru in June and wanted her report to be about something "useful." He leaned over the counter now, tapping the Sahara graph. "Pick a desert," he said. "It'll demonstrate that you understand harsh places, not just vacation spots."

"I'm doing both. That's the assignment." She spun the globe and started sticking small green flags on every major desert she could find. Sahara. Arabian. Kalahari. Australian outback. Atacaca. She stepped back and frowned. "That's not random. They're not scattered everywhere. They line up."

Her dad came around the counter. "Line up how?"

Samantha hunted through the desk drawer until she found the strip of latitude tape Aunt Rosa used for planning routes. She laid it across the globe at thirty degrees north and checked it against her flags. Every flag in the Northern Hemisphere sat on or near the band. She moved the tape to thirty degrees south. Kalahari. Australian outback. The flags matched again. "Two belts," she said. "The hot deserts all sit near thirty degrees north or south of the equator."

"Why there?"

"Doesn't matter for my report." But she pulled the agency's weather binder off the shelf anyway, because the teacher had warned her that a graph without a reason was just decoration. The binder's climate chapter had one line that stopped her: at those latitudes, air sinks, and sinking air warms up and dries out. She copied the page number onto her hand, then dragged the rainfall graph for the Amazon next to the Sahara graph and built her foundation paragraph: the rainforest sits on the equator and gets soaked all year, while the deserts sit in the thirty-degree belts where the air dries everything out, so their rainfall bars barely exist and their temperatures swing wild between day and night.

Aunt Rosa came back from the printer and looked over her shoulder. "You just solved in twenty minutes what took me a semester."

"Can I keep the flags until Monday?"

"Keep the globe." Aunt Rosa slid it across the counter. "Bring it back with the A."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Nevaeh had sold exactly four tubs of cookie dough for the robotics club fundraiser, and the club needed to know the total by Friday. Mr. Ruiz's spreadsheet assignment was due the same day, so she decided to combine the two problems into one. She opened her laptop in the media center, typed the four names into column A, and put the dollar amounts into column B: 12, 8, 15, and 10.

"Now the formula," said Marcus, sliding into the chair beside her. He was already done with his chart and kept leaning over. "You type equals, SUM, then the range in parentheses."

"I know," Nevaeh said, though she didn't. She typed =SUM(B2:B5) the way he had said it, and pressed Enter. The cell filled with 45. That matched her own addition, which she had done on paper first, because she trusted paper.

She highlighted the four amounts and clicked the chart button. Four bars appeared, and the tallest one belonged to Priya, who had sold the 15 dollars' worth. Nevaeh dragged the chart next to the numbers and sat back. It looked finished, almost authentic, like something a real club treasurer would send out.

Then Priya herself walked by the table on her way to the printer. "That says I did fifteen," she said, pointing at the chart. "It was nineteen. Devon wrote it down wrong." Nevaeh checked her order form. Priya was right. She braced herself to redo everything, the sum and probably the chart too, the way she would have on paper. But first she changed the 15 to a 19 in cell B4, just to see.

The total became 49. Nobody had typed the formula again. The total had become 49 all by itself, and the tall bar grew taller while she watched. Nevaeh stared at the screen, then typed 15 back in, and the total dropped to 45 again. She changed it to 19 once more and left it there. "It fixes itself," she said. "The SUM watches the whole range."

"So you don't have to redo the math," Marcus said.

"Which is the whole irony of me doing it on paper first," Nevaeh said. She saved the file, attached it to an email for the club president, and wrote in the subject line: Total is 49, and it will still be right if someone finds another typo. Then she printed a copy for Mr. Ruiz, and the chart came out of the printer with Priya's bar reaching nearly to the top of the page.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
story:
Lucas stood at the long steel counter with three clocks ticking in his head: rice in twenty minutes, curry in thirty, flatbread whenever he could manage it. His uncle had given him the Saturday night station because the usual cook had a fever, and last Saturday, when Lucas had been too nervous to try, he had spent the whole shift washing pots. He wasn't going to spend this one washing pots.

He started the rice first, since it took longest, then the curry, chopping onions while the pot hissed. The flatbread dough had been resting in a bowl since noon, soft rounds dusted with flour. He had watched the cook slap them onto the hot pan a hundred times, but he had never actually made one puff up himself. Sometimes they ballooned like little moons, and sometimes they just sat there, flat and sad, and he had never figured out why. He had a guess, though. His friend Dev had stood at the kitchen door last month, staring, and said, "It puffs because there's water in the dough, and the water turns into steam." Lucas had filed that away without really believing it. Steam was invisible. How could you trust a cause you couldn't see?

He decided to be systematic about it. He took two rounds of dough. One he rolled thin and left alone. The other he patted with wet fingers before laying it on the pan, working a few drops of water into the surface. If the steam idea was right, the wet one should do something the dry one wouldn't. He laid both on the hot steel and waited, spatula ready.

The dry round browned quietly, staying flat. The wet one lifted at the edge, trembled, and then ballooned so fast it startled him, swelling into a fat golden dome. Lucas laughed out loud. Dev had been right, and now Lucas had seen it happen twice in a row, which felt different from hearing it once. He flipped the puffed one, pulled both off, and started a third, wetting this one deliberately and pressing it gently with a cloth so the steam had somewhere to push from. It rose even rounder than the first.

By the time the rice was done, he had six puffed flatbreads stacked under a towel and the curry bubbling at a steady simmer, everything landing together at the pass like a rehearsal that had actually worked. His uncle leaned over the counter, eyed the stack, and raised an eyebrow. "You've been holding out on me, pot washer."

"I figured out the bread," Lucas said. "It's not luck. I did it on purpose." He knew his uncle ran this kitchen like a monopoly and rarely handed anyone a station twice, so this night mattered more than one dinner. Whether he would get the flatbread station again next Saturday was still undecided, and Lucas found he wasn't sure he wanted it as much as he'd thought an hour ago. He slid the last dome onto the stack and called through the window, "Order up."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
story:
Leo's essay was due Monday morning, and by Saturday afternoon he had one paragraph, which his teacher had already crossed out because it said "heaven is where you go after you die, probably." The assignment was to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and Grandpa, who was Christian, had taken him to a burial at church last month, so that half was easy. The other half was the problem, until the phone rang.

"Anil's father passed this morning," Grandpa said, setting down the receiver. "The ceremony is at four. Come along, and keep your eyes open. And put on a shirt with a collar."

The Rao family lived three doors down, and their yard was full of neighbors by the time Leo and Grandpa arrived. At the far end, on a bed of wood, lay Mr. Rao's father, covered in flowers. Anil, who ran the corner store and knew Leo by name because of the ice cream budget, stood beside it, steady and quiet. His uncle touched Leo's shoulder and spoke near his ear. "We cremate our dead. The body goes back to the five elements."

Leo's hand went to his pocket, where he had a folded page of notes for the essay. Five elements. He wrote it later on the back of a bulletin from Grandpa's church, squeezed between two folding chairs: body returned to five elements. At church, the casket had gone into the ground, and the pastor had talked about resurrection and a permanent home with God. Two very different pictures, and his essay could finally stand up on both legs.

Then Anil walked him to the back fence, where a small mound of fresh earth lay under the guava tree, ringed with marigolds. "My son," Anil said. "He was six. We didn't cremate him." Leo didn't ask why, but Anil went on anyway, his voice even. "Young children we bury. Some holy people too." He knelt and set a flower on the mound. "Different, even inside one faith. Your essay will say that, I hope."

"It will now," Leo said.

That night Grandpa read the draft at the kitchen table, tapping the page with one finger. "You wrote that Anil's ice cream revenue dropped this month. What's that got to do with anything?"

"Context," Leo said, and Grandpa laughed so hard he had to put down his coffee.

On Monday Leo handed it in, and on Wednesday the teacher read one line out loud to the class: "Maybe no one can see past death directly, so every faith builds its own bridge." After school, Grandpa was waiting by the gate with the car already running.

"Ice cream," Grandpa said. "Anil's buying."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and coffee, because the gym was a polling station today and Aria's civics class had been sent to run a student vote beside the real one. Her job was the Charter table. She had to get a voter to read one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in their own words, then write the explanation on a card for the class wall. Her teacher wanted ten cards by lunch. She had two.

The cards she had were thin. One man had read "everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person" and written "be safe," which was not going to pass. Aria stared at the photocopied Charter pages taped to the table and noticed something she had skipped before. Beside section 15, the equality rights, someone had written a date: 1985. Every other section said 1982.

"Grandma," she called across the table, where her grandmother stood in line for the real ballot. "Come here a second."

Grandma waved at the returning officer and stepped over, still holding her voter card. "Make it quick, they'll call my name."

Aria pointed at the page. "Why does this one say 1985? The rest say 1982."

Grandma squinted. "Section 15?"

"Equality rights. Equal protection and equal benefit of the law, without discrimination."

"Ah." Grandma tapped the number with one finger. "That one came into force in 1985. Three years after the rest."

"Three years? Why would a right be late?"

"Governments needed time to update their laws. All the old laws had to be changed to match it."

Aria wrote that down, fast, because the line was moving and a poll worker was already calling "next voter." Grandma squeezed her shoulder and went to get her ballot, and Aria sat with the fact turning in her head like a coin. Three years. The right existed on paper but waited, on purpose, so everything else could catch up.

She tested the idea out loud on the next student voter, a boy from her math class wearing a candidate's campaign button that had saturated overnight with rain, the blue ink bleeding into the white. "Pick a section," she said. "Any one."

He shrugged and jabbed at random. Section 15.

"Okay. Read it. Then tell me what it means, your words, not the book's."

He read it twice, lips moving. "It means the law can't treat you worse because of, like, who you are. And everybody gets the same protection from it."

"Good. Now the weird part." She showed him the dates. "This one started in 1985, three years after the rest. The other rights came in 1982. They gave the governments time to update their laws first."

He frowned at the page. "So they knew the laws were unfair, and they left them unfair for three more years?"

"That's not what it says."

"Feels like it, though."

Aria didn't answer. She took his card, looked at his plain words beside the delayed date, and pinned both to the class wall, where the equality card hung apart from the conventional row of 1982 sections, alone at the end of the line.

"Pins are in the cup," the boy said, and slid them across to her.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Brayden tapped his pencil against the rainfall graph for the Sonoran Desert, then against the one for the Amazon rainforest, and felt his stomach drop. Mr. Okafor had promised that whoever made the best comparison poster would get to present it at the seventh-grade science assembly, and Brayden wanted that spot more than he had wanted anything since he made the travel team. The problem was that every poster in the room looked the same so far: a cactus, some trees, two graphs, done. His wasn't going to be done. His was going to be right.

"Your rainforest line just sits there," said Priya, leaning over from the next desk. "Did you plot it wrong?"

"No, look." Brayden traced the temperature graph for the Amazon with his finger. The line hardly moved all year. The desert line, though, swung up in the summer and plunged in the winter like a roller coaster he would never be brave enough to ride. "The desert changes month to month way more. That's the whole comparison. Hot place that varies, hot place that doesn't." He wrote that on his poster and felt pretty good about it for almost ten minutes.

At lunch, his little sister Elena texted him a photo of her duffel bag, half packed, because she was leaving Friday on a school trip to Ecuador. Guess what, it said, we're going to a rainforest reserve. Then: what do I pack? Brayden typed back shorts obviously, it's hot every month, and hit send. He was the science poster kid. He knew things. Somewhere outside the cafeteria window, a kid was running a vigorous lap around the track, and Brayden watched him without really seeing him, because something was itching at the back of his mind.

That night he pulled up the climate data again, and this time he didn't skip past the second sheet, the one labeled hourly readings. The desert graph he'd memorized showed month to month. This sheet showed something else: day by day. And the rainforest's daily line jumped high at noon and sank low at midnight, over and over, a sawtooth. He grabbed a ruler and measured. The wiggle between day and night in the rainforest was bigger than the flat little yearly change on his poster. He sat back so fast his chair squeaked. He texted Elena before he could talk himself out of it. Bring a sweater. For nights. Trust me.

The next morning he rebuilt the poster around it. He found a photo of a rainforest rodent, some agouti-looking thing, curled against a leaf, and captioned it warm days, cold nights, and he made the sawtooth line the biggest thing on the page so nobody could miss it. Priya read it twice. "I thought rainforests were just hot," she said slowly. "So did I," Brayden said. "I told my sister not to bring a sweater. I was wrong." Saying it out loud felt like stepping on a scale in front of the whole class, but Priya just nodded and said, "That's the best poster in here."

Friday after school, Elena's first photo from the reserve came through: her, grinning in the dark, wrapped in a sweatshirt with the hood up, a caption underneath that said you were right, I'm freezing. Brayden laughed out loud in the kitchen, then screenshotted it and printed it in color for the corner of his poster, right beside the sawtooth line. Then he slid the poster into his backpack, carefully, flat against his books, so it wouldn't bend before the assembly.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
story:
Jordan sat cross-legged on the damp-smelling carpet of Marcus's basement, laptop warm on his knees, while the dehumidifier hummed in the corner like a sleepy robot. On the screen was his very first web page, and it was a disaster. Every single word, the heading and all three paragraphs about his dog Biscuit, had transformed into one enormous bold line that stretched past the edge of the screen. Marcus leaned over his shoulder, chewing a pretzel.

"I didn't type it like that," Jordan said. "I typed h1 in brackets before the heading, just like the tutorial."

"Then type it again and watch," Marcus said, flicking a pretzel salt off the trackpad.

Jordan retyped it, slower this time, and the page still looked like a giant had shouted across it. He sat back and stared. The computer was doing something invisible to him, something he couldn't see, and it had to have a rule behind it. Last summer, he remembered, the city pool had turned green overnight and nobody could figure out why until the lifeguard tested the water and found the chemical balance was off. Invisible cause, visible mess. He had liked that day, in a strange way. He scrolled up and down his code, looking for his own invisible cause.

Near the top he found the tutorial's example: opening tag, then words, then a second tag with a slash inside the brackets. His own code had the first two but not the third. He checked every line. "Most of these come in pairs," he said slowly. "Opening tag, then content, then a closing tag with a slash." He said the words out loud because saying them made the pattern feel real. "Mine never closes."

"So fix it," Marcus said, mouth full.

Jordan typed the slash and the letters into the closing tag, wrapped around his heading like a bun around a hot dog, and saved. The page reloaded and the heading snapped to the top, normal-sized, with his paragraphs sitting neat and ordinary underneath. He pumped his fist and knocked over the pretzel bag, which was pretty much a toxic spill as far as Marcus was concerned, since his mom had just vacuumed.

"Now center it," Marcus said, sweeping salt with his hand. "The tutorial said CSS."

Jordan added the style rule with "text-align: center" and saved again. The heading slid to the middle of the page, balanced and tidy, like it had always belonged there. Marcus squinted at it, then at the code, then at the screen again.

"Do another page," Marcus said. "One about the basement. I'll get more pretzels."

story:
Kaylee had exactly forty minutes of lunch period to make her page look like the one in Grandpa's old web tutorial, which he had printed out in 1998 and mailed to her in an envelope that smelled faintly of his garage. The tutorial was three pages long, held together with a staple gone rusty orange like lichen on a rock. She spread it beside the keyboard in the computer lab and typed the first line the way it said: a heading, wrapped in a tag called center, with angle brackets around it.

"Is that a real thing?" asked Desmond, sliding into the seat beside her with his sandwich. He leaned over, chewing. "Center. In brackets."

"It's in the tutorial." Kaylee saved the file and hit refresh. The heading sat there, dead centre, exactly like the picture. She sat back, satisfied for about four seconds. Then she noticed the little orange flag in her editor, sitting at the end of the line like a tiny warning lighthouse. She clicked it. A message popped up telling her the tag was deprecated in HTML 4, in favour of the CSS text-align property.

"Deprecated," Desmond read aloud. "Is that like deported?"

"It's like retired." Kaylee frowned at the screen. The page worked. Grandpa's tutorial worked. And yet the editor was acting like she'd done something embarrassing. She scrolled through the message again, but it was opaque on one point: it never said what she was supposed to do instead, only what had replaced it. CSS. She'd heard of CSS. Somewhere in her binder was a worksheet with the word on it, probably near the bottom, probably unfinished.

She found the worksheet. There was a curly-brace thing with the word text-align inside it and a colon after it, like the code was introducing itself at a party. She couldn't see how a style connected to a heading, though. The tags were invisible in the browser; whatever linked them had to be invisible too. So she tested it. She typed the curly-brace rule, aimed it at her heading, deleted Grandpa's center tag, and saved, holding her breath like the file might object.

Refresh. The heading stayed centred.

"It worked," she said. "Without the old tag."

Desmond peered at the screen, then at the tutorial, then back. "So Grandpa's instructions are antique."

"They worked, though." She looked at the orange flag again. Still there, pointing at nothing now, because she'd already fixed the line it had been complaining about. She realized the flag had been there from the beginning, waiting, and she'd only noticed it because the page had loaded and given her those four satisfied seconds. Somewhere in that gap between "it works" and "it works the right way" was a lesson she decided not to think too hard about yet.

She emailed Grandpa a screenshot of the finished page, heading dead centre, with the subject line "Your tutorial still works." Then she added a second screenshot, the one with the orange flag, and typed underneath: "But look what the editor thinks of your tag." She pressed send and watched the little envelope icon fly off the corner of the screen.

"He's going to write back in all caps," Desmond said.

"He thrives on it," said Kaylee, and closed Grandpa's tutorial, rusty staple and all.

story:
Zachary slouched in front of the lab computer and stared at his web page. The heading, "Zachary's Skate Spot," sat crammed against the left edge like it was hiding from the rest of the screen. Everything else looked fine, the photos, the list of his favourite boards, even the paragraph about the time he broke his wrist. So why did the heading hug the wall?

"Yours is the only one stuck in the corner," said Priya from the next seat. She leaned over. On her screen, her heading floated right in the middle. "I don't know how mine got there, though. I typed a bunch of stuff and it just happened."

That was the part that bugged Zachary. Something invisible was moving these headings around, some rule hidden in the code. He scrolled through Priya's stylesheet line by line, hunting for anything she had that he didn't. There it was, buried near the bottom: h1 { text-align: center; }. He'd read the words but never tested them. What if the tag name at the front was a target, and the curly-brace part was an instruction aimed straight at it?

He copied it into his own stylesheet and hit refresh. His heading slid to the middle of the page like it had been waiting for permission. Zachary grinned. Then he wondered something else. His page had a second big heading, lower down, above his board collection. He scrolled. That one had moved to the middle too. So the rule wasn't about one heading, it was about all of them, every top-level heading on the whole page.

"Whoa," he said. "One line moved both of mine."

Priya spun her chair around. "Both? Show me." He added a third h1 near the bottom as a test, and it appeared dead centre as well. She laughed. "So that's why mine worked. I thought I'd done something wrong and it fixed itself."

Their teacher, walking past, paused behind them. "Finding the lab computers a fertile place for experiments this morning?"

"Sort of," Zachary said. "I'm keeping a list of every rule that actually works, so next time I'm not guessing. Might end up like a little database of CSS."

"Smart," she said, and moved on.

Priya frowned at her own screen. "My quiz scores fluctuate so much, I need that database more than you do."

"Then help me test the next one," Zachary said, and typed a new line.

story:
Naomi sat cross-legged in the reading nook under the attic window, photocopy of Macbeth in one hand, phone in the other. Marcus was coming over in forty minutes, and their English group had to turn the scene into modern English by tomorrow. She had read the page three times and still could not tell what the witches were saying.

"Doth," she muttered. "Hath. What is that." She flipped the photocopy over and found the paraphrase worksheet. Scene one, line by line, blank spaces waiting. Marcus would have his part done. Priya already had hers. Naomi wrote "she hath the witch's power?" and crossed it out. Guessing felt like throwing darts in the dark.

She tried something instead of guessing. She circled every word that ended in -eth or -th: doth, hath, speaketh, knoweth. Four of them, all sitting where a normal verb would sit in the sentence. She wrote "she hath" on a sticky note, then underneath, "she has." It fit. She tested it on the next one: "the wind doth blow" became "the wind does blow." That fit too. Every single one worked if she swapped doth for does and hath for has. It was a pattern, like a lock clicking open. She pulled the sticky note onto the wall of the nook and labeled it RULE, in case it stopped working later.

The doorbell rang. Marcus dropped his backpack by the stairs and climbed up into the nook, holding out his sheet. "I got most of it. Some of it. Okay, two lines." Priya texted that she was sick and would send her part by morning, which left the hard speech for the two of them. Naomi handed him the sticky note. "Read this first."

He read it twice. "So doth means does? That's it? And hath means has?" Naomi slid the photocopy across to him and tapped the circled words. "Show me one place it doesn't work. I couldn't find any." Marcus squinted, mouth moving, then grabbed the pencil. He wrote fast, almost knocking over her water bottle, and held up the sheet. "'The witches knoweth the future' becomes 'the witches know the future.' Right?" Naomi nodded and took the pencil back. "Then let's finish this speech before it gets dark." Outside the window, the wind rattled the gutter, and Marcus said quietly, "The wind doth blow," and grinned.
